chapters.title: Chapter 5: Applying Duration and Convexity as an Indian Investor

lessons.title: Matching Duration to Your Goal: Immunisation for Retail Investors

children.text: You need ₹16.5 lakh in about seven years for your daughter's engineering fees. You have ₹10 lakh today and G-Secs yield 7%. The maths says it works. But between now and then, RBI will cut rates, raise them, or both, and every one of those moves changes both your bond's price and the rate at which your coupons get reinvested. Is there a way to make the outcome safe regardless? There is, and you already have every tool needed to see why it works. It rests on one instruction: match the duration of your bonds to the length of your goal.

body.text: Set your portfolio's Macaulay duration equal to your investment horizon, and rising yields hurt your prices by almost exactly what they add to your reinvestment income. The two risks cancel, and your final sum becomes predictable.

markDefs.definition: Structuring a bond portfolio so that its value at a target date is protected from interest rate changes, by setting its Macaulay duration equal to the investment horizon.

children.text: Chapter 2 showed that falling rates hurt reinvestment but help prices, and rising rates do the reverse.

exploits that tug of war. Hold a bond for too short a time and the price effect dominates: a rate rise leaves you selling at a loss before your coupons have earned enough to make up for it. Hold it for too long and reinvestment dominates: a rate fall means years of coupons earning less. There is exactly one holding period where the two effects offset, and it is the bond's Macaulay duration.

body.caption: The immunisation condition. Note it uses Macaulay duration, measured in years, not modified duration.

children.text: Does It Actually Work? A Test

Take an illustrative 10-year G-Sec with a 7% coupon, priced at par at a 7% yield. Its Macaulay duration is 7.355 years. Invest ₹10 lakh, and set the horizon at exactly 7.355 years. Now suppose yields jump or collapse the day after you buy and then stay there. Coupons are reinvested at the new yield, and whatever bond remains is sold at the horizon at that yield. For comparison, run the same test with a 20-year bond (duration 11.05, too long) and a 3-year bond whose proceeds are reinvested until the horizon (too short).

body.caption: Value of ₹10 lakh after 7.355 years, under an immediate one-off change in yields

body.title: Value at the Goal Date After a One-Off Yield Shock (₹ lakh)

children.text: The matched line is almost flat. Across a four percentage point range of yields, the outcome varies by ₹3,470 on ₹16.6 lakh, about two tenths of one percent. The 20-year bond swings by nearly ₹2.4 lakh and the 3-year by nearly ₹3 lakh, in opposite directions. The mismatched portfolios are bets on rates. The matched one is not.

body.label: The counterintuitive part
body.context: Coupons pull duration well below maturity, so matching a horizon to a bond's maturity leaves you badly mismatched. Match duration, not maturity.

body.title: Why the offset works, step by step

children.text: Suppose yields jump from 7% to 9% the day after you buy. Two things happen at once. Your bond's price falls immediately, so if you sold today you would lose. But every coupon from now until the goal date is reinvested at 9% instead of 7%, and the bond you still hold at the goal date will have a shorter remaining life, so its price will have recovered most of the way back towards par.

The size of the price loss depends on duration. The size of the reinvestment gain depends on how long you have left to reinvest, which is your horizon. Set those two equal and the effects cancel to a first approximation. They do not cancel perfectly, which is why the matched row varies by a few thousand rupees rather than zero, and convexity is the reason the small residual is always in your favour: notice that the matched outcome at 5% and at 9% is slightly higher than at 7%.

body.title: Build a duration-matched portfolio
body.prompt: You have a goal exactly 5 years away. You can buy a 2-year G-Sec with a Macaulay duration of 1.9 years and a 10-year G-Sec with a Macaulay duration of 7.355 years. What percentage of your money should go into the 2-year bond to immunise the goal? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Solve w × 1.9 + (1 − w) × 7.355 = 5. So w = (7.355 − 5) ÷ (7.355 − 1.9) = 2.355 ÷ 5.455 = 0.432, or 43.2% in the 2-year bond and 56.8% in the 10-year. Portfolio duration is a weighted average, exactly as in Chapter 3.

children.text: The Simplest Immunisation: No Coupons at All

There is one instrument that immunises perfectly with no maths at all: a zero-coupon bond maturing on your goal date. Its duration equals its maturity, so matching is automatic, and with no coupons there is nothing to reinvest. Whatever rates do in between, you receive the face value on the day you need it. In India that means a T-bill for goals within a year, or G-Sec STRIPS for longer goals, subject to availability through your platform.

body.title: Two Ways to Defuse Rate Risk

columns.label: Duration matching (immunisation)
points: Set portfolio Macaulay duration equal to the horizon
Works with ordinary coupon bonds you can actually buy
Needs rebalancing as time passes and yields move
Protects against roughly parallel shifts in the curve
Leaves a small residual, which convexity makes favourable

columns.label: Cash flow matching
points: Hold instruments whose payments land when you need the money
A zero-coupon bond maturing on the goal date is the pure case
No rebalancing needed once it is set up
Immune to any yield curve movement, not just parallel ones
Limited by what is available: STRIPS, T-bills, target maturity funds

body.title: Pick the right structure
body.question: Ravi needs ₹20 lakh in exactly 3 years for a house down payment, and he wants as little uncertainty as possible. Which structure fits best?
options: A long duration gilt fund, because gilt funds carry no credit risk
A 10-year G-Sec held for 3 years and then sold
Instruments whose cash flows land at the 3-year mark, such as a target maturity fund maturing then, or a G-Sec portfolio with a Macaulay duration of about 3 years
A perpetual AT1 bond, because the coupon is high
body.explanation: A 3-year horizon needs about 3 years of duration. A 10-year G-Sec has a duration of about 7.4, so selling after 3 years exposes Ravi to whatever yields do. A long duration gilt fund is worse still: no credit risk does not mean no rate risk. The AT1 bond adds credit, call and extension risk on top.

children.text: What Indian Investors Can Actually Use

body.caption: Practical ways to match duration to a goal in India

cells: Target maturity funds and index funds with a fixed maturity date
Portfolio rolls down towards a stated maturity, so duration shrinks as your goal approaches
Pick a maturity date close to your goal; check the index, expense ratio and whether you must hold to maturity
A G-Sec on RBI Retail Direct maturing near the goal
Principal arrives when you need it; only coupons need reinvesting
Coupon reinvestment still leaves some uncertainty, and duration is shorter than maturity
T-bills (goals within a year) and G-Sec STRIPS (longer)
Zero-coupon, so duration equals maturity and nothing is reinvested
STRIPS availability and liquidity for retail buyers can be limited
A debt fund chosen by its Macaulay duration
SEBI categories are defined by Macaulay duration, so you can pick a band that matches
Managers change duration; recheck the factsheet, as Chapter 3 showed
Bank FD maturing on the goal date
Fixed value at a fixed date, with no price risk at all
DICGC cover is ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank; premature withdrawal penalties apply

body.text: Target maturity funds are the closest thing Indian retail investors have to easy immunisation. A fund maturing in 2030 holds G-Secs, SDLs or PSU bonds maturing around that date, and its duration falls automatically as the date nears, just as a matched portfolio should. Bharat Bond ETFs, launched from December 2019, made this structure widely available. Match the fund's maturity year to your goal year and most of the work is done for you.

children.text: Immunisation is not a one-time setup. A year after you buy, your horizon has shortened by a full year, but your bond's duration has not. Our 10-year bond starts with a duration of 7.355 years; a year later, as a 9-year bond, its duration is 6.826 years, while the horizon is down to 6.355. The portfolio is now 0.47 years too long, and the gap widens every year. Duration also changes when yields move. Practical fix: check once a year and shift a little into shorter bonds when the gap grows, or use a target maturity fund that rolls down on its own.

body.text: Immunisation protects against yield levels, not against everything. It assumes yields move in roughly parallel fashion, so a sharp twist in the curve can still leave a gap. It assumes the issuer pays: a defaulted corporate bond is not immunised by any duration. And it protects a rupee amount, not purchasing power, so a goal whose cost rises with inflation, such as college fees, is only partly addressed by a fixed sum.

body.title: Name the strategy
body.textWithBlank: Setting a bond portfolio's Macaulay duration equal to the investment horizon, so that price risk and reinvestment risk offset, is called ___.
body.explanation: The term comes from making the portfolio immune to interest rate changes over a specific horizon. It works because the two interest rate risks pull in opposite directions and are equal in size at exactly the Macaulay duration.

body.title: Sandeep funds a college bill
body.scenario: Sandeep Nair, a 46-year-old marine engineer in Kochi, has ₹30 lakh set aside and needs roughly ₹45 lakh in about seven years, when his son starts an engineering degree. His bank relationship manager suggests a long duration gilt fund with a modified duration of 9.2, pointing to its strong recent returns. His own research turns up a target maturity index fund maturing in seven years with a portfolio YTM of 7.15% and a Macaulay duration of 5.6 years, and a 10-year G-Sec on RBI Retail Direct yielding 7.05% with a Macaulay duration of 7.35 years.
body.prompt: Assess each option against Sandeep's goal, say which structure best immunises it, and list what he should still check.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Long duration gilt fund, modified duration 9.2: far longer than his seven-year horizon. If yields fall he does well, and if they rise in year six he may be badly short at exactly the wrong moment. Its recent returns describe a past rate cycle, not his future. Reject on horizon mismatch.
2. 10-year G-Sec, Macaulay duration 7.35 years: almost exactly matched to a seven-year horizon. This is textbook immunisation. He would need to reinvest coupons and check the match every year or two as duration drifts.
3. Target maturity fund maturing in seven years, duration 5.6 now: its duration is shorter than his horizon today, but it rolls down automatically and returns the money at the maturity date, which is cash flow matching rather than duration matching. For a fixed date goal this is arguably the cleanest option, with no reinvestment or rebalancing work for him.
4. Does ₹30 lakh reach ₹45 lakh? At about 7% compounded for seven years, ₹30 lakh grows to roughly ₹48 lakh before tax, so the goal is achievable with a margin, provided he does not take rate risk that could leave him short.
5. What he should still check: (a) the tax treatment of debt fund gains versus G-Sec interest, with his CA; (b) the target maturity fund's index, credit quality and expense ratio; (c) whether fees will actually be ₹45 lakh, since education costs inflate faster than headline inflation, so he may want to revisit the target; (d) liquidity if he needs part of the money early; (e) that he has not concentrated everything in one instrument or one issuer.
6. Suggested approach: use the target maturity fund as the core because it matches the date without maintenance, and treat the G-Sec as an equally valid alternative if he prefers to hold the security directly.

body.title: Immunising a goal in seven steps
steps: Write down the goal date and the rupee amount you need.
Convert the goal date into a horizon in years.
Calculate the Macaulay duration of the bonds or funds you are considering.
Choose holdings whose weighted Macaulay duration equals the horizon, remembering that duration is shorter than maturity.
Prefer cash flow matching where you can: a zero-coupon instrument or a target maturity fund ending at the goal date.
Reinvest coupons promptly, since immunisation assumes it.
Recheck the match once a year, because duration falls more slowly than time passes.
Confirm credit quality, and treat inflation in the goal amount as a separate question.

points: Immunisation means setting portfolio Macaulay duration equal to your horizon, so price risk and reinvestment risk offset.
In our test, the matched portfolio's value varied by ₹3,470 across a 4 percentage point yield range, against ₹2.4 lakh and ₹3 lakh for mismatched ones.
Match duration, not maturity: a 7.4-year goal calls for a 10-year coupon bond.
A zero-coupon instrument maturing on the goal date immunises perfectly, with no reinvestment and no rebalancing.
Duration drifts: after one year our matched bond was 0.47 years too long, so the match needs an annual check.
Target maturity funds roll down automatically and are the most practical route for most Indian investors.
Immunisation covers yield levels, not curve twists, defaults or inflation in the goal amount.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or tax advice. Bonds, funds, yields and investors are illustrative, and the immunisation test assumes a single immediate parallel shift in yields with coupons reinvested at the new rate. Real outcomes depend on the path of yields, curve shape, credit events, costs and taxes. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
